summary: Describes an architecture for describing SNMP management frameworks. It is a standards-track document. It obsoletes RFC 2271 and was replaced by RFC 3411.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the blueprint showing which parts make up a network-monitoring system and how they fit together.

questions: what are the snmpv3 security levels
subtitle: The modular blueprint that names the parts of an SNMP management system and how they fit together.

tldr.problem: SNMP needed a shared vocabulary and structure so that message formats, security and access control could be replaced or upgraded piece by piece, with secure SET support as the main gap in earlier versions.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture splits an SNMP entity into an engine (dispatcher, message processing, security and access control subsystems) plus applications, and defines the names, abstract interfaces and a MIB module that connect them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2571 obsoletes RFC 2271 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3411, so the current version of this architecture is in that later document.

today: RFC 2571 is a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3411, which now carries this architecture. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2271.

sections.title: Goals and Design Decisions
sections.content:
This document defines a vocabulary for describing SNMP Management Frameworks and an architecture for their major parts. It is not a general introduction to SNMP and not a history. It uses the requirement words of RFC 2119.

The goals include reusing existing work (it is heavily based on SNMPv2u and SNMPv2*, which came from SNMPv2p), addressing the need for secure SET support, which it calls the most important deficiency in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, keeping SNMP as simple as possible, and making it cheap to deploy a minimal implementation while still supporting large networks.

The design decisions follow from that. Subsystems are defined by abstract service interfaces. Each document is self-contained, so pieces can move along the standards track on different timelines. Security and access control parameters must be remotely configurable. The RFC stresses that this modularity of specification does not impose requirements on how implementations are built.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors wanted a toy set made of separate blocks, so you can swap one block for a better one later without rebuilding the whole thing.

sections.title: Threats a Security Model Must Address
sections.content:
The architecture sorts threats by importance. A Security Model SHOULD protect against the two principal threats, modification of information and masquerade, and against the secondary threats of message stream modification (malicious re-ordering, delay or replay) and disclosure (eavesdropping).

It need not protect against denial of service, since such attacks are often indistinguishable from the network failures that any management protocol must cope with, or against traffic analysis, since management traffic patterns are often predictable.

The Security Considerations section adds that the level of security depends on the Security and Access Control Models chosen, that applications SHOULD take reasonable steps to protect data from disclosure, and that the purchaser of an implementation is responsible for checking that it meets their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The guards must stop people from changing letters or pretending to be someone else, and should stop copied or snooped messages. They do not have to stop someone from simply blocking the road.

sections.title: Entities, Engines and Applications
sections.content:
An SNMP entity is an implementation of the architecture: one SNMP engine plus one or more applications. The engine, identified by its snmpEngineID, provides services for sending and receiving messages, authenticating and encrypting them, and controlling access to managed objects. It contains four parts: a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem.

The Dispatcher sends and receives messages on the network, finds the version of each message and hands it to the matching Message Processing Model, and gives applications an abstract way to receive or send PDUs. The Message Processing Subsystem can hold several models, one per message format. The Security Subsystem can hold several Security Models, such as the User-Based Security Model, and the Access Control Subsystem can hold several Access Control Models, such as the View-Based one.

Applications include command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. An entity with command generators or notification receivers is traditionally called a manager, and one with command responders or notification originators is traditionally called an agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a post office: a counter that receives and sends mail, a clerk who reads each envelope, a security guard, and a rule keeper who decides who may see what. The people asking questions and answering them are the customers.

sections.title: Naming Identities, Contexts and Security Levels
sections.content:
A principal is the who on whose behalf processing takes place. It is represented by a securityName, a human-readable string that does not depend on any Security Model. Each Security Model maps between that name and its own model-dependent security ID, such as a community name or user name.

Management information is named with a context: a collection of information accessible by an SNMP entity. A context is identified by a contextEngineID plus a contextName, which must be unique within the entity. A scopedPDU bundles those two names with a PDU. To find, say, the description of device-X's first interface, you need the engine ID, the context name, the object type ifDescr and the instance.

Every message also has a securityLevel, one of three ordered values: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. All subsystems and applications are REQUIRED to supply or respect it.
sections.plainLanguage: To find one fact you need the right building, the right room in it, and the right shelf. A security level is how strong the lock on the envelope is.

sections.title: Abstract Service Interfaces
sections.content:
The architecture describes how the pieces talk through primitives, such as sendPdu for an application sending a request, prepareOutgoingMessage and prepareDataElements for message processing, and generateRequestMsg and processIncomingMsg for security. There are also primitives for access control and for registering which application handles a given type of PDU.

The RFC says these interfaces describe externally observable behavior, are not constraints on how implementations are structured, and must not be read as APIs. Scenario diagrams show a command generator sending a request and later receiving the response, and a command responder registering, receiving a PDU and returning a response.

The document also classifies PDUs by function (read, write, response, notification, internal) and by whether a response is expected (confirmed or unconfirmed), using RFC 1905 operations as examples. Section 5 defines MIB objects used to instrument SNMP entities in this architecture, and Appendix A gives design guidelines for new models.
sections.plainLanguage: The parts pass notes to each other in a fixed way. The notes show who does what, not exactly how you must build each part.

sections.title: IANA Number Spaces
sections.content:
The document defines three number spaces for IANA to manage. Security model values 0 to 255 are for standards-track models, with 0 reserved for any, 1 for SNMPv1, 2 for SNMPv2c and 3 for the User-Based Security Model (USM). Message processing model values also run from 0 to 255, with 0 for SNMPv1, 1 for SNMPv2c, 2 for SNMPv2u and SNMPv2*, and 3 for SNMPv3.

The third space is for SnmpEngineID formats: the fifth octet is a format identifier, and the values managed by IANA run from 6 to 127.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of lock and each kind of envelope gets its own number, written in an official list so nobody picks the same number twice.
